title: Your first month abroad: a checklist from people who just did it
seoTitle: First month abroad checklist for Indian students (2026)
description: First month abroad checklist for Indian students: the first 48 hours, week one admin and official visa steps for the UK, USA, Canada, Australia and more.
excerpt: What to do in your first 48 hours, first week and first month abroad, from a mentor who moved to Leeds in 2024, with official steps for six countries.
keywords: checklist for international students after arrival
things to do after arriving in UK as a student
study abroad packing list from India
imageAlt: Three students laughing together around a wooden table with laptops and notebooks

author.name: Priya Sharma
author.role: Mentor, MSc Data Science, University of Leeds
author.bio: Priya Sharma moved from Hyderabad to Leeds in 2024 for an MSc in Data Science and now mentors Indian students getting ready for their first year abroad.

takeaways: Keep every important document in one hand-luggage folder, with offline copies on your phone.
Photograph your room against the inventory before you unpack. It protects your deposit.
Each country has a first-month legal step, from the UK eVisa to Germany's Anmeldung. Read the official page for yours.
Check the hours limit on your own visa before you take any part-time job.
If the first weeks feel heavy, reach out early. Most universities offer free, confidential counselling.
faqs: What should I do first after arriving abroad as a student?

In the first 48 hours, get a working SIM, tell your family you have arrived, reach your accommodation and photograph your room against the inventory. Then eat and rest. Leave enrolment, banking and immigration steps for your first week, and do two or three tasks a day.
Do I need a National Insurance number before I start work in the UK?

Not always. GOV.UK says you can start work before you receive your National Insurance number if you can prove your right to work in the UK. If you do not already have one, you can only apply once you are in the UK, and it can take up to four weeks to arrive.
How soon do I need to do Anmeldung in Germany?

The Federal Registration Act says you must register within two weeks of moving into your home. The DAAD notes that some local offices expect it sooner, so book an appointment early. Keep the registration confirmation, because you need it for your residence permit.
When can an F-1 student apply for a Social Security number?

Only once you have authorised employment, such as an on-campus job, and after speaking to your DSO. Study in the States advises waiting 10 days after arriving and making sure your SEVIS record has been Active for at least two days before you apply.
When do I register my immigration permission in Ireland?

Immigration Service Delivery says you must register within 90 days of arriving in Ireland. You book an appointment with the Registration Office, and your Irish Residence Permit card is posted to you afterwards. If you cannot get an appointment within 90 days, the official page says your permission will not be cancelled while you wait.
Is university counselling free for international students?

At most universities, yes. Counselling and wellbeing services are usually free and confidential for all enrolled students, including international students. Check your own university's wellbeing page to confirm and to see how to book.
How do I avoid rental scams when moving abroad?

Never pay a deposit for a room that you or someone you trust has not seen, and be wary of landlords who say they are abroad and cannot show the property. Use your university accommodation service or established letting agents and pay by traceable methods. A price far below everything else nearby is a warning sign.

source:
When I landed in Leeds in September 2024, I had two suitcases, a folder of printouts and a list my cousin had written on the back of an envelope. Half of it was useful. The other half I learned the slow way: queueing at the wrong desk, paying for a SIM plan I did not need, and eating toast for three nights because I had not found the Indian grocery yet.

This is the list I wish I had been given, built from my first month and from what TYM mentors in the USA, Canada, Australia, Ireland and Germany told me about theirs. The everyday steps are similar everywhere. The immigration and tax steps are not, so for those I have linked the official page for each country. Rules change, so treat those links as the final word.

## Before you fly: build one folder {#before-you-fly}

Almost everything in your first week depends on documents. Keep them in one folder in your hand luggage, never in the checked bag. If your suitcase goes to the wrong city, you can manage without clothes for two days. You cannot enrol without your papers.

- **Passport** with your visa or permit details, plus a photocopy of the photo page.
- **Study confirmation**: CAS for the UK, Form I-20 for the USA, letter of acceptance and port of entry letter for Canada, CoE for Australia, admission or acceptance letter for Ireland and Germany.
- **Offer letter** and any scholarship or sponsor letters.
- **Financial proof** you used for the visa, such as bank statements, a loan sanction letter or blocked account confirmation.
- **Accommodation contract** with your hall's or landlord's contact details.
- **Prescriptions** for medicine you carry, a doctor's letter, and the medicine in its original packaging.
- **Degree certificates and transcripts**, as some universities check originals at enrolment.

Then make offline copies. Scan every page into a phone folder that opens without internet, and email a set to yourself and one parent. When I had no signal at Manchester airport, the offline PDF of my accommodation confirmation was how I showed the taxi driver where I was going.

:::tip Keep a paper list of phone numbers
Write five numbers on paper: a parent, a friend already abroad, your accommodation, your university's international office and the Indian embassy or consulate in your new country. Phones die and get lost at the worst moments.
:::

### Money for the first few days

Carry a little local currency for day one: enough for a train or taxi, a meal and a SIM top-up. After that, use a forex card or an international debit card from your Indian bank until your local account is open. Tell your bank you are travelling so your first payment abroad is not blocked, and keep a backup card in a different bag.

### Pack what is actually hard to find

Rice, dal and most spices are easy to find abroad. Harder to replace quickly: a pressure cooker you trust, a tawa, your usual brand of medicines, plug adapters, and warm clothes for weather you have never lived in. Check your destination's customs rules before packing food. Some countries are strict about seeds, meat, dairy and fresh produce, so declare food when in doubt.

## The first 48 hours: arrive, connect, sleep {#first-48-hours}

The first two days are not for admin. They are for landing safely, telling people you are fine and getting your body into the new time zone.

:::steps
Get connected | Buy a local SIM or set up an eSIM at the airport or in town. You need a local number for your bank, your doctor and most university forms. Keep your Indian number active for OTPs from Indian banks.
Tell your family you have landed | Message them when you land and call once you reach your room. Agree a rough calling time for the first week so nobody panics while you sleep.
Get to your accommodation | Use the route your university or accommodation recommends. Many universities run airport pick-ups or welcome desks at the start of term.
Check your room and photograph everything | Before you unpack, walk through the room with the inventory. Photograph stains, scratches, the mattress and the inside of the fridge, then email the photos to your landlord or hall office the same day so there is a dated record.
Eat, then sleep | Eat a proper meal and go to bed at a normal local bedtime, even if you feel wide awake. Jet lag fades faster when you follow local daylight.
:::

On deposits: in England and Wales, if you rent privately on an assured shorthold tenancy, your landlord must put your deposit in a government-approved [tenancy deposit protection scheme](https://www.gov.uk/tenancy-deposit-protection) within 30 days of receiving it. Other countries have their own rules, so ask your university accommodation office. Everywhere, the photos from day one are what settle a dispute.

:::checklist First 48 hours
Documents folder in my hand luggage, offline copies on my phone
Local SIM or eSIM working, Indian number still active
Family told I have landed safely
Reached my accommodation and collected the keys
Room checked against the inventory and photographed
Photos emailed to my landlord or hall office
Found the nearest supermarket and pharmacy
Ate a proper meal and slept at a local bedtime
:::

## Your first week: the admin week {#first-week}

By day three the excitement settles and the queues begin. Write a short list each morning and finish two or three things a day. Trying to do everything on Monday is how you end up close to tears in a queue, which I did, briefly, outside the student hub.

### University enrolment and student ID

Finish online enrolment, then collect your student ID card in person. At many universities this is also where staff check your passport and immigration status. Your student card gets you into the library and often qualifies you for student prices.

### Open a bank account

Requirements vary, but you will usually need your passport, proof of immigration status and proof of address. With no bills in your name yet, ask student services for a letter confirming your enrolment and address, which many banks accept. App-based banks can be quicker while you wait for a branch appointment.

### Transport and student discounts

Ask the students' union which travel discounts exist. Most cities have student fares, monthly passes or railcards, and some universities, particularly in Germany, include a transport ticket in the semester fee. Sign up for student discount schemes only through official apps and websites.

### Find the Indian grocery store

Ask in the [UK community](/c/uk) or the community for your country. Seniors know which shop has fresh curry leaves and which is cheaper for atta. I found mine in my second week and immediately felt less far from home. If faith matters to you, look up the nearest temple, gurdwara, mosque or church too.

### Register with a doctor

Do not wait until you are ill. In England you can [register with a GP surgery](https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/gps/how-to-register-with-a-gp-surgery/) online for free, and the NHS says you do not need ID, proof of address or proof of immigration status. Elsewhere, your university health centre or international office will explain how student health cover works and which clinic to use.

:::checklist First week
Enrolment completed and student ID collected
Started the immigration step for my country (see the table below)
Bank account application submitted
Transport card or student pass sorted
Registered with a GP, campus clinic or local doctor
Found the nearest Indian grocery store
Went to at least one society or student event
Wrote down my weekly budget
:::

## Country-specific must-dos for your first month {#country-must-dos}

These steps differ by country. I checked each against the official page linked in the table, but rules change, so read your own visa or permit conditions before you act. Your university's international office has answered all of these questions before.

:::stats
14 days | Germany: register your address after moving in (Federal Registration Act)
90 days | Ireland: register your immigration permission after arriving
30 days | England and Wales: landlord must protect your tenancy deposit
:::

:::table
Country | First-month must-do | Where to do it
UK | Sign in to your UKVI account and check your eVisa shows the right details and passport. eVisas have replaced physical documents such as BRPs. If you plan to work and have no National Insurance number, apply once you are in the UK. Register with a GP. | [GOV.UK: eVisas](https://www.gov.uk/evisa), [GOV.UK: National Insurance number](https://www.gov.uk/apply-national-insurance-number), [NHS: register with a GP](https://www.nhs.uk/nhs-services/gps/how-to-register-with-a-gp-surgery/)
USA | Contact your designated school official (DSO) as soon as you arrive, and no later than the programme start date on your I-20. Keep a full course of study. Apply for a Social Security number only once you have authorised employment, such as an on-campus job. | [Study in the States: maintaining status](https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/students/maintaining-status), [Study in the States: getting an SSN](https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/students/obtaining-social-security-number)
Canada | Apply for a Social Insurance Number before you start work, as you need one to work. Your study permit must carry conditions that allow work. Stay enrolled and keep making progress in your programme. | [Service Canada: SIN for temporary residents](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/sin/temporary-residents.html), [IRCC: study permit conditions](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/study-permit/while-you-study/study-permit-conditions.html)
Australia | Apply for a Tax File Number online once you are in Australia; it is free. Keep your Overseas Student Health Cover active, as it must cover you from the day you arrive. | [ATO: TFN for temporary visitors](https://www.ato.gov.au/individuals-and-families/tax-file-number/apply-for-a-tfn/foreign-passport-holders-permanent-migrants-and-temporary-visitors-tfn-application), [Home Affairs: Student visa (subclass 500)](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-listing/student-500)
Ireland | Book an appointment and register your immigration permission within 90 days of arriving. Your Irish Residence Permit (IRP) card is then posted to you. | [Immigration Service Delivery: registering for the first time](https://www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/how-to-register-your-immigration-permission-for-the-first-time/information-on-registering-your-immigration-permission-for-the-first-time/)
Germany | Register your address (Anmeldung) at the residents' registration office within two weeks of moving in and keep the confirmation. Then apply for your residence permit at the local foreigners' authority (Ausländerbehörde). | [Federal Registration Act, section 17](https://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/bmg/__17.html), [DAAD: registration and residence permit](https://www.study-in-germany.com/en/germany/arrival/residence-permit/)
:::

### Details that catch people out

- **UK:** your UKVI account gives you a share code when an employer or landlord asks you to prove your status. GOV.UK says you can start work before your National Insurance number arrives if you can prove your right to work, and that the number can take up to four weeks.
- **USA:** Study in the States advises waiting 10 days after arriving before applying for an SSN, with your SEVIS record Active for at least two days. Talk to your DSO first.
- **Canada:** a temporary resident's SIN starts with a 9 and expires with your immigration document. You can only start working once your study programme has started.
- **Australia:** you must be in Australia to apply for a TFN online, so do it early and have it ready before your first payday.
- **Ireland:** if you cannot get an appointment within 90 days, the official page says your permission will not be cancelled while you wait. A registration fee may apply, depending on your permission.
- **Germany:** the DAAD says many registration offices expect you within one or two weeks, so book early. You need the registration confirmation (Meldebestätigung) for your residence permit.

:::cta community

## Money, budgeting and cooking {#money-and-food}

I will not give you prices. They differ hugely between Leeds and London, Toronto and Halifax, Munich and Leipzig, and any number I wrote would be wrong for most of you. Here is the method that worked for me and most mentors I asked.

:::steps
Start with the total | Write down the money you have for the term: savings, family support and any scholarship. Do not count money from a job you do not have yet.
Take out the fixed costs | Subtract rent, tuition instalments, your phone plan, a transport pass and insurance.
Divide by weeks | Divide what is left by the weeks until more money arrives. That is your weekly budget for food, toiletries, going out and everything else.
Track for four weeks | Note every spend in a notes app or spreadsheet and compare it with your weekly figure every Sunday. Week one will run over while you set up your room. That is normal. Adjust in week two.
Keep a buffer you do not touch | Hold a separate emergency amount for a lost phone, a doctor's bill or a sudden trip home.
:::

My biggest leaks were takeaways after late labs, buying kitchen things one at a time instead of at second-hand sales, and converting every price into rupees, which made me either panic or overspend. Stop converting after the first fortnight and think in your weekly figure.

### Cooking basics that save money and homesickness

Learn five dishes before you fly: dal, a dry sabzi, rice, a simple chicken or paneer curry, and a breakfast that is not cereal. Cook them once with whoever cooks at home and write down the quantities. Abroad, batch-cook on Sunday and freeze portions for deadline weeks. Cooking with flatmates is also the easiest way to make friends. I met two of my closest friends over a pot of rajma neither of them had tried before.

## Part-time work: check your visa first {#part-time-work}

Almost everyone wants a part-time job in month one. Before you apply, read the work conditions on your own visa or permit and check the hours limit on your visa. Limits depend on the country, your level of study and whether it is term time, and breaking them can put your visa at risk. Read them from the source:

- UK: [Student visa: what you can and cannot do](https://www.gov.uk/student-visa/what-you-can-and-cannot-do), and the conditions in your eVisa.
- USA: [Study in the States: maintaining status](https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/students/maintaining-status). F-1 students may only work when authorised, so ask your DSO first.
- Canada: [IRCC: work off campus as an international student](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/study-canada/work/work-off-campus.html).
- Australia: [Home Affairs: Student visa (subclass 500)](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/visas/getting-a-visa/visa-listing/student-500).
- Ireland: the conditions of your immigration permission, from [Immigration Service Delivery](https://www.irishimmigration.ie/registering-your-immigration-permission/).
- Germany: [BAMF: studying in Germany](https://www.bamf.de/EN/Themen/MigrationAufenthalt/ZuwandererDrittstaaten/Bildung/Studium/studium-node.html).

Start with your university careers service and campus job board. Campus employers understand timetables, and the careers team can rework your CV into the local style. Never take cash-in-hand work that hides your hours. It feels harmless until it is not.

## Making friends and dealing with homesickness {#friends-and-wellbeing}

Nobody warns you that the first month can be lonely even when you are surrounded by people. Everyone else looks settled. They are not. Welcome week is the easiest time to meet people, because everyone is new.

- Join two societies: one connected to home, like the Indian society, and one that has nothing to do with your course or country.
- Say yes to the first three invitations, even the ones that sound boring.
- Keep your kitchen door open while you cook. It sounds silly. It works.
- Talk to coursemates before and after lectures, not only in the group chat.

> Keep your friends from home close, because they will feed you during exams, but sit next to someone new at least once a week. That is how I found my study group, and that group got me through second semester.
> — Daniel Okafor, Mentor, BEng Computer Engineering, Toronto Metropolitan University

### When homesickness hits

It often arrives in week two or three, when the excitement fades and the first assignment lands. For me it was a Sunday evening when I realised nobody around me knew it was Dussehra. What helped was a fixed call time with home, cooking something familiar, getting outside in daylight, and telling one friend in Leeds how I actually felt.

If low feelings last more than a couple of weeks, or you stop sleeping, eating or going to class, please talk to someone. Most universities run a counselling or wellbeing service, and at most universities it is free and confidential for students. Find your university's wellbeing page in week one so you know how to book before you need it. Asking for help is not a weakness. It is like seeing a doctor for a fever.

:::warning If you feel unsafe
If you might hurt yourself or you are in danger, call the local emergency number straight away: 999 in the UK, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 112 or 999 in Ireland, and 112 in Germany.
:::

## Staying safe and spotting scams {#safety-and-scams}

Most student cities are safe if you use the same sense you would at home. Share your live location with a friend on late nights, use licensed taxis or ride apps, and learn the route between campus and home in daylight first.

### The scams that target new international students

- **Fake landlords.** A room is listed far below nearby prices, the owner is conveniently abroad, and they want a deposit before you can view it. Do not pay for a place that you or someone you trust has not seen.
- **Fake visa or tax calls.** A caller claims to be from immigration or the tax office and says you must pay now or be deported. Hang up. Canada's immigration department says it will never ask you for payment by telephone, and HMRC says it will never ask for personal or payment information by text message.
- **Bank account and job scams.** Offers to pay you for moving money through your account, or jobs that charge a fee upfront. Either can get your account closed and land you in legal trouble.
- **Fake fee requests.** Emails asking you to pay tuition into a new account. Pay only through your university's official portal.

:::warning Before you send money to anyone
Stop, wait an hour and ask a senior or your university advice service. Scammers rely on panic. In the UK you can [report suspicious HMRC calls, texts and emails](https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/hm-revenue-customs/contact/reporting-fraudulent-emails), and in Canada IRCC explains how to [protect yourself from fraud](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship/services/protect-fraud.html).
:::

## Ask people who were there last year {#tym-community}

Every question here has been asked in a TYM community, usually at midnight by someone sitting next to unopened suitcases. Join your country community before you fly: [UK](/c/uk), [USA](/c/usa), [Canada](/c/canada), [Australia](/c/australia), [Ireland](/c/ireland) or [Germany](/c/germany). Search first, then [ask a question](/ask) if nobody has.

If you want someone to walk through your first month with you, [book a mentor](/mentors) who studied in your city. For quick questions at odd hours, [ask TYM AI](/ai) and check the answer against the official links above. Still on your application? Read our guides to [UK visa funds](/blogs/uk-visa-funds-explained) and [SOP openings](/blogs/sop-openings-that-work).

:::cta mentor

Your first month will not go perfectly. Mine did not. But by week four I had a bank card, a GP, a favourite bench by the library and a group chat that argued every evening about biryani or pasta. You will get there too, probably sooner than you think.

title: Five SOP openings that admissions teams actually remember
seoTitle: How to start an SOP: 5 statement of purpose openings (2026)
description: How to start your SOP: five statement of purpose openings with original examples, the openings to avoid, and a checklist to use before you submit.
excerpt: Five ways to open a statement of purpose that readers remember, with original examples, the openings to avoid and a checklist for before you submit.
keywords: how to begin a statement of purpose
statement of purpose for MS in US
imageAlt: A mentor and a student reviewing a printed statement of purpose draft together at a table

author.name: Sara Thomas
author.role: Mentor, MS Information Systems, Northeastern University
author.bio: Sara Thomas applied from Kochi without a consultant, got into four of six US programmes with a partial scholarship, and now reviews SOPs for TYM students applying to information systems and analytics courses.

takeaways: Your opening should be specific enough that it could only belong to you.
Five shapes work well: a live problem, a failure and the fix, a real number, a genuine question, or an honest bridge from an unusual background.
Skip famous quotes, childhood clichés, definitions, achievement lists, flattery and tragedy used as a hook.
Rewrite the 'why this programme' section for every application, and follow each programme page's prompt and limit.
Cut the first paragraph you wrote, read the draft aloud, and get a reader who does not know you.
faqs: How should I start my SOP?

Start with something specific from your own work or study: a problem you are working on, a failure and what you changed, a number from a project, a question you keep asking, or an honest explanation of an unusual background. Avoid general statements about your interest in the field. The reader should learn something concrete about you within the first two sentences.
How long should the opening paragraph of an SOP be?
Three to five sentences is usually enough. In a shorter UK personal statement, two or three sentences may work better. The opening should set up your story, not tell all of it.
Can I start my SOP with a quote?
You can, but it rarely helps. A famous quote spends your most valuable line on somebody else's words, and readers have seen the popular ones many times. Open with your own experience instead.
Should I mention a gap year or backlog in my SOP?

Yes, if you handle it briefly and honestly. A gap year can be part of an opening if you explain what you did with it. Backlogs are usually better addressed calmly later in the SOP or in an additional information section, along with what you did to improve.
What is the difference between an SOP and a UK personal statement?

Both explain why you want to study a programme, but UK personal statements are often shorter and more focused on academic preparation and interest in the course, while US statements of purpose often give more room to goals and programme fit. Requirements vary by university, so always follow the prompt and limit on the course page.
Should I write a different SOP for each university?

Your opening and most of your experience section can stay similar, but the section on why you chose the programme should be rewritten for each application. Mention modules, labs or research areas specific to that programme, and check that no other university's name is left in the draft.
Can I use AI to write my SOP?

Using a tool for feedback on clarity is different from having it write your SOP. Some universities now state their position on AI use in applications, so check the guidance for each one. Readers can usually tell when an SOP sounds generic, and your own specific details are what make it work.
source:
I have read a lot of Statements of Purpose. Some were my own drafts, many more belonged to juniors from Kochi and Thrissur who messaged me after I got into Northeastern, and since becoming a TYM mentor I have read SOPs from students applying everywhere from Dublin to Munich. The pattern that still surprises me is how often a strong applicant writes a weak first paragraph.

When I applied, I did it without a consultant. I rewrote my opening more times than I want to admit, sent my SOP to six US programmes, and got offers from four, one with a partial scholarship. I do not think the opening got me in. I do think a better opening made the people reading my file pay attention to the parts that did. This guide is what I wish someone had told me about those first few lines, with original example openings you can study and adapt, and the openings I now ask students to delete.

## Why the first paragraph carries so much weight {#why-the-opening-matters}

Think about who reads your SOP. It is usually a small committee or a programme team working through a large pile of applications in a short season, often alongside their teaching and research. They are not looking for reasons to reject you, but they are busy, and they have seen the same kind of opening many times. Nobody can tell you exactly how long they spend on each file, and I would be wary of anyone who quotes a precise figure. Common sense is enough: a reader who is bored by line three reads the rest faster.

Your opening has one job. It should make the reader think, 'this person has done something real and knows why they want this degree.' That is all. It does not need to be poetic, clever or emotional. It needs to be specific enough that it could only have been written by you.

A useful test: cover your name, swap your opening paragraph with a friend's, and ask whether anyone could tell the difference. If your paragraph would fit in any other applicant's SOP, it is not doing its job yet.

:::tip The specificity test
Underline every noun in your opening. If most of them are abstract (technology, innovation, society, field, dream), rewrite. If most of them are concrete (a warehouse in Aluva, an error rate, a Python script, a district hospital), you are on the right track.
:::

Below are five openings I have seen work again and again, across countries and subjects. Each example is one I wrote for this article, based on the kind of experiences Indian applicants actually have. Please do not copy them. Borrow the shape, then fill it with your own facts.

## Opening one: the problem you are already working on {#opening-a-problem-you-are-working-on}

The strongest openings often start in the middle of work you are already doing. Not a dream, not a childhood memory, but a real problem you have noticed, tried to solve, and not fully solved yet. The unsolved part matters, because it is the reason you need the degree.

:::example Example opening
At the logistics firm in Kochi where I work as a junior analyst, our delivery estimates for monsoon weeks are often wrong by almost a full day. I built a simple model that adjusts for rainfall forecasts, and it narrowed the error, but I could not explain why it failed badly in two districts. I want to study supply chain analytics because I have reached the edge of what I can teach myself, and I would like to understand that failure properly.
:::

**Why it works.** In three sentences the reader learns your current role, a concrete problem, what you already tried and an honest limit. It also sets up the rest of the SOP naturally: your experience, the gap in your knowledge, and why this programme fills it.

**How to adapt it.** List three problems you noticed at work, in a project or during an internship that annoyed you enough to try fixing. Pick the one most closely tied to the programme. Write one sentence on the problem, one on what you tried and one on what you could not solve. If you are a final-year student, a lab project or a college fest that kept running over budget can work just as well as a job.

**When not to use it.** Skip this opening if the problem has nothing to do with the course, or if you would have to exaggerate your role. If you were an intern who watched a project rather than worked on it, say so, or choose a different opening. Readers spot inflated ownership quickly.

## Opening two: the moment something failed and what you changed {#opening-a-failure-and-what-you-changed}

Failure openings work when the focus is on what you changed afterwards, not on how bad you felt. Admissions readers want evidence that you can learn, and a well-told mistake is some of the best evidence there is.

:::example Example opening
In my third year of engineering, the soil moisture sensor our team built for a farmer in Palakkad stopped working within a week. We had tested it in the lab, never in clay soil during a dry spell. I spent the next semester rebuilding it with a field test at every stage, and the second version ran for four months. That project taught me I enjoy testing even more than building, which is why I am applying for a master's in embedded systems with a focus on reliability.
:::

**Why it works.** It shows honesty, a specific fix and a lesson that points straight at the programme. The failure is small and practical, which makes it believable. You are not asking for sympathy; you are showing how you think when something goes wrong.

**How to adapt it.** Choose a failure where you were responsible for at least part of the outcome, and where you can name what you did differently next time. Keep the failure to one sentence and spend more words on the change. End the paragraph by connecting the lesson to the subject you want to study.

**When not to use it.** Avoid it if the failure raises questions you cannot answer in a few lines, such as a backlog you have not explained elsewhere. Backlogs and gaps are worth addressing, but usually in a calm paragraph later in the SOP or in an additional information section, not as your first impression. Also avoid any failure story that blames teammates, professors or the system.

## Opening three: a concrete number from your own work {#opening-a-number-from-your-work}

A single number, used honestly, makes your work feel real. It tells the reader that you measured something, which is what most postgraduate programmes will ask you to do every week. My own SOP opened with a number, though a clumsier one than the example below. It was the paragraph every early reader of my draft commented on first, which told me it was doing its job.

:::example Example opening
The attendance tracker I built for my college's placement cell cut the time our coordinators spent on weekly reports from about six hours to forty minutes. It was a small project, a shared spreadsheet, some scripting and a lot of trial and error, but it was the first time I saw how much a team's week could change because someone organised its data properly. I want to study information systems so that I can do this for a hospital or a city, not just a college office.
:::

**Why it works.** The number is modest and believable. It comes with context (what the tool was and who used it) and with a reason it mattered. The final sentence turns a small college project into a direction.

**How to adapt it.** Look for numbers you can defend if someone asks: hours saved, users served, accuracy improved, cost reduced, samples tested, students taught. Round sensibly and say 'about' when you are estimating. One number is enough. Three numbers in the first sentence reads like a CV.

**When not to use it.** Do not use a number you cannot explain in an interview, or one that belongs to the whole team while you present it as yours. And do not force a number into a subject where it feels unnatural. For a master's in public policy or literature a number can still work, but a question or a moment may suit you better.

## Opening four: the question you could not stop asking {#opening-the-question-you-keep-asking}

Some applicants are driven less by a single project and more by a question that keeps coming back. This opening suits research-leaning programmes and anyone thinking about a PhD later, because it shows curiosity with a direction.

:::example Example opening
While volunteering at a government school in Madurai, I noticed that students who did well in Tamil-medium maths tests often struggled when the same questions were set in English. I started keeping notes on which words tripped them up, and after two terms I had a list of forty terms that seemed to cause most of the confusion. I still do not know whether the problem is vocabulary, confidence or the way the tests are written, and that is the question I want to spend a master's in education research trying to answer.
:::

**Why it works.** The question comes from something observed, not from a textbook. The writer has already started answering it with simple notes, which shows initiative. And the last line is honest about what they do not know, which is exactly where a good postgraduate student starts.

**How to adapt it.** Write the question down in plain words first, without any jargon. Then ask yourself where you first noticed it and what you have done about it since. If the answer is 'nothing yet', this opening will feel thin. Pick another one, or go and do something small about the question before you write.

**When not to use it.** Avoid it for strongly industry-focused programmes where readers want practical outcomes, unless your question is practical too. And never open with a rhetorical question such as 'Have you ever wondered how the internet works?' A real question is one you are asking yourself, not one you are asking the reader.

## Opening five: the bridge from an unusual background {#opening-a-bridge-from-an-unusual-background}

If your path looks unusual on paper, such as a commerce degree followed by a data science application, three years in sales before a management master's, or a gap year, the reader will notice. The best thing you can do is address it in your first paragraph, plainly and without apology.

:::example Example opening
I studied commerce at a college in Thrissur and spent my first two years after graduation reconciling invoices for a mid-sized textile exporter. The work was repetitive, so I taught myself Python in the evenings to automate it, and within a year the finance team was using my scripts every month. That is how a commerce graduate ended up applying for a master's in data science: not because I left accounting behind, but because accounting is where I first learnt what messy data costs a business.
:::

**Why it works.** It answers the reader's first question before they can ask it. It turns the unusual background into an advantage, a domain the applicant understands better than many computer science graduates would. And the tone is matter of fact, which reads as confident.

**How to adapt it.** Name where you started, the moment you began moving towards the new subject, and the evidence that the move is real: a course, a project, a tool you built, a role you took on. For a gap year, say what you did with it in one factual sentence, whether that was preparing for an exam that did not work out, caring for a parent or working in a family business. Then move to what you learnt or built during it.

**When not to use it.** If your background is not actually unusual for the programme, you do not need a bridge, and spending the opening on one wastes space. Do not over-explain either. A gap year needs one or two honest sentences, not a paragraph of justification. If the reason is personal or medical, you can mention it briefly without details.

## Openings to avoid, and why they fall flat {#openings-to-avoid}

Every admissions season I see the same six openings. None of them will get you rejected on their own, but each one wastes the most valuable space in your SOP. Here they are, with short weak examples I made up, so you can recognise them in your own draft.

### The famous quote

:::example Weak opening
'The only way to do great work is to love what you do.' These words have guided me throughout my life.
:::

The reader has seen this quote, and others like it, many times. It tells them nothing about you, and it hands the first line of your SOP to somebody else.

### The 'since childhood' line

:::example Weak opening
Since childhood, I have been fascinated by computers and how they work.
:::

Almost every applicant could write this sentence. It also pushes your story back fifteen years when the reader wants to know what you have done recently. If a childhood memory truly matters, put it later and keep it to a line.

### The dictionary definition

:::example Weak opening
The dictionary defines data science as the study of data to extract meaningful insights.
:::

The committee knows what their own subject is. A definition signals that you were not sure how to begin, so you borrowed a sentence.

### The list of achievements

:::example Weak opening
I am a first-class graduate with a CGPA of 8.9, two published papers, three internships and a national hackathon finalist certificate.
:::

Your transcript and CV already say this. Repeating it in the opening turns your SOP into a second CV. Pick one of those achievements and tell its story instead.

### Flattering the university

:::example Weak opening
Your esteemed university, with its world-class faculty and rich heritage, is the perfect place for me to pursue my dreams.
:::

Praise without detail reads as copied, because it could be sent to any university. Save your reasons for choosing the programme for later in the SOP, and fill them with specific modules, labs and research areas.

### Tragedy used for effect

:::example Weak opening
When my grandfather passed away in a hospital that lacked basic equipment, I knew I had to become a healthcare data analyst.
:::

Real loss can shape what people choose to study, and I am not saying you must hide it. But when a tragedy is used as a hook, it often feels like it is there to move the reader rather than to explain your choice. If it truly matters, mention it briefly and honestly later in the SOP, and let your actual work carry the opening.

:::cta mentor

## What comes after the opening

A strong opening with a weak middle is still a weak SOP. Once your first paragraph is working, the rest should follow one clear line of thought. This is the structure I give most students. It is not the only one, but it is hard to go wrong with it.

:::steps
The work so far | Two or three paragraphs on your education, projects, internships and jobs, chosen because they connect to the programme. For each one, say what you did, what you learnt and what it led to. Cut anything that does not connect, however proud you are of it.
The gap | One short paragraph on what you cannot do yet and why. This is the honest bridge between your experience and the degree, and a clear gap makes the next section believable.
Why this programme specifically | Name modules, labs, research groups or faculty research areas that match your gap. Research them on the programme's own pages, read a few recent project or publication titles, and explain how they fit what you want to learn. Do not just list them, and do not name a professor unless you have read their work and can say something sensible about it.
What you will do after | Describe a realistic next step, such as a role, a sector or further research, and, where it fits, how it connects to India or to your field more widely. Specific and modest beats grand and vague.
Closing | Two or three sentences that return to your opening problem, failure, number or question and show where you hope to take it. Do not summarise the whole SOP, and do not end with a quote.
:::

:::warning Do not send one SOP to every programme
Your opening and your experience paragraphs can stay mostly the same across applications. The section on why you chose this programme must be rewritten for each one. Readers can tell when a university's name has been swapped into a template, and a wrong name left in by mistake is far worse.
:::

> When I review an SOP, I ask one thing of every paragraph: could the reader check this? If you say you led a project, name what you built. If you say a module excites you, say which one and why. Specific sentences are the ones people believe.
> — Priya Sharma, Mentor, MSc Data Science, University of Leeds

## How the US, UK, Germany, Canada and Australia differ {#country-differences}

The word 'SOP' gets used for everything, but the documents vary by country and by programme. The table below is a general guide based on what I and other TYM mentors have seen. It is not a rulebook. Always follow the instructions, prompts and word or character limits on each programme's own application page, because they change from year to year and can differ between departments in the same university.

:::table
Country | What it is usually called | What tends to matter
United States | Statement of purpose, sometimes alongside a separate personal history statement | Academic and professional goals, research or project fit, and why this specific programme. Some programmes set prompts or limits; follow them exactly.
United Kingdom | Personal statement or supporting statement | Often shorter and focused on your academic preparation and interest in the course. Some programmes ask specific questions in the application form instead. Always follow the word limit on the course page.
Germany | Motivation letter (Motivationsschreiben) | Usually more formal and closely tied to the course content and your academic background. Some universities publish guidance on what to include, so check each programme page and the international office's pages.
Canada and Australia | Statement of purpose, statement of intent or personal statement, depending on the university | Varies widely between universities and between research and coursework degrees. Check whether the programme gives a prompt, and keep your career plans clear and realistic.
Ireland | Personal statement or statement of purpose | Often submitted through the online application form. Check the course page for length and any specific questions.
:::

A few things hold everywhere. Readers want evidence rather than adjectives, a clear reason for choosing this programme, and a plan that makes sense. The five openings above work across all of these formats. In a shorter UK personal statement, your opening may need to be two sentences instead of four, but the same shapes still apply. If you are heading to the UK, our guide to [UK visa funds](/blogs/uk-visa-funds-explained) covers the money you will need to plan for alongside your applications.

## An editing process that actually works {#editing-before-you-submit}

First drafts of SOPs are almost always too long, too general and too polite. Here is the process I use with students, and the one I used on my own.

### Cut the first paragraph you wrote

Most first paragraphs are warm-up. Writers clear their throat, describe their interest in general terms, and only reach the real story in paragraph two. Delete your first paragraph and see whether the SOP gets better. Surprisingly often, your second paragraph is your real opening.

### Read it aloud

Read the whole SOP aloud, slowly, ideally to an empty room. You will hear the sentences that run too long, the words you repeat and the phrases that sound like nobody you know. If you would not say a sentence to a senior over chai, rewrite it.

### Ask 'so what' after every sentence

Go through the SOP one sentence at a time and ask, 'so what?' If a sentence does not tell the reader something about your ability, your motivation or your fit, it is either missing its second half or it should go. 'I completed an internship at a fintech startup' needs a second half: what did you do there, and what did it change about your plans?

### Find a reader who does not know you

Your parents, friends and college professors know your story, so they fill in the gaps without noticing. A reader who does not know you will show you where you lose them. Ask them to mark the first line where they got bored, and the one sentence they remember after a single read. Fix the first and protect the second.

### Check the limit last, but check it properly

Write freely first, then cut to the limit. Check whether the programme counts words or characters, whether spaces count, and whether each question has its own limit. If no limit is given, keep it focused; a longer SOP is not a stronger one. Finally, paste the text into the application portal and check that your paragraph breaks and special characters survived.

:::checklist Before you submit your SOP {#before-you-submit-your-sop}
My opening paragraph could only have been written by me
The opening has at least one concrete detail: a place, a project, a number or a real question
There are no famous quotes, dictionary definitions or childhood clichés
Every paragraph connects to the programme I am applying to
The section on this programme names modules, labs or research areas I have actually read about
The university and programme names are correct everywhere, with nothing left over from another application
My plans after the degree are specific and realistic
I have read the SOP aloud from start to finish
Someone who does not know me has read it and told me where they lost interest
It meets the exact prompt and the word or character limit on the programme page
:::

### Getting a second reader

If you do not have a senior who has been through this, that is exactly why TYM exists. You can [book a mentor](/mentors) who studied in the country you are applying to. [Priya Sharma](/mentors/1) reviews SOPs line by line and is especially good at catching vague sentences, and you can book time with me, [Sara Thomas](/mentors/4), if you are applying for information systems, business analytics or similar programmes in the US.

If you want quick feedback before a full review, you can [ask TYM AI](/ai) to read a draft and point out generic lines. It is a useful first pass, but treat it as a second opinion rather than a final word, and never let any tool rewrite your SOP into somebody else's voice. You can also [ask a question](/ask) or browse the [US community](/c/usa) and [UK community](/c/uk), where students share what worked for them and what did not.

:::cta community

Once you have submitted, the waiting begins, and then, with luck, the planning. When an offer arrives, our [first month checklist](/blogs/first-month-checklist) covers what to sort out after you land. Until then, write the opening only you could write, and make every paragraph after it earn its place.

faqs: How much bank balance do I need for a UK student visa from India?

At the time of writing, your outstanding first-year course fees plus £1,529 a month for a London course or £1,171 a month outside London, for up to nine months. For a one-year master's that is £13,761 or £10,539 in living costs on top of fees. Subtract fees already paid and any qualifying university accommodation deposit, and check GOV.UK for the current figures.
Can I show my parents' bank account for a UK student visa?

Yes. Money in a parent's or legal guardian's account counts, as long as they control the account. You also need a letter from them consenting to you using the money, and proof of the relationship, usually your birth certificate showing their name.
Can my brother, uncle or grandparent show funds for my UK student visa?

No. For a Student visa the account must be in your name (alone or jointly), your parent's or legal guardian's name, or your partner's if they are applying with you or already have permission. If a relative is helping, move the money into an eligible account and wait the full 28 days before you get your statement.
Does the 28-day rule apply to education loans?

No. If you rely on an education loan, you upload a loan letter instead, dated within six months of your application and meeting the UKVI conditions, including that the loan is to you and has no conditions other than a successful visa application. Any part of the total not covered by the loan must still be shown in an account that meets the 28-day rule.
Do Indian students need to submit financial documents for a UK student visa?

Yes. At the time of writing India is not on the GOV.UK differential evidence list, so Indian nationals should upload full financial evidence with the application. Students from listed countries still have to hold the money and can be asked to prove it.
What happens if my bank balance drops after I apply?

Ideally, leave the money untouched until you have a decision. If the balance is substantially lower when the caseworker checks, they must be satisfied it went on course fees, an accommodation deposit or other costs of your studies. Keep receipts for anything you pay.
Is the London rate based on where I live or where I study?

Where you study. If more than half of your course is taught in the City of London or the 32 London boroughs, you use the London figure, even if you live outside London. A course outside London uses the lower figure even if you commute from London.

source:
Ask any family sending a child to the UK what worries them most, and it is rarely the course or the IELTS score. It is the bank statement. The money was there, the offer was real, and the visa still came back refused because the balance dipped for two days in July, or the savings sat in an uncle's account, or the statement was a week too old. One technicality, and the fee and several weeks are gone.

The reassuring part is that the funds rule is mostly mechanical. There is a number, a 28-day window, a 31-day deadline, and a short list of people whose money counts. Get those four right and this part of your application is in good shape. Every figure below is correct at the time of writing and checked against GOV.UK, but these figures change, so check the linked pages before you finalise anything.

## How much money you need

You add two things together: your outstanding course fees and a fixed monthly amount for living costs. Flights, the visa fee and the health surcharge are not part of this number.

### Part one: outstanding course fees

You need the fees for one academic year, or for the whole course if it is shorter. For a one-year master's, that is usually the full tuition fee. The figure that counts is the one on your Confirmation of Acceptance for Studies (CAS). Anything already paid to the university comes off. If a payment is not on your CAS because you paid afterwards, upload the university's receipt.

### Part two: living costs

At the time of writing, [GOV.UK](https://www.gov.uk/student-visa/money) asks for **£1,529 a month for courses in London** and **£1,171 a month outside London**, for each month of the course up to nine months. A one-year master's needs all nine: **£13,761 in London** or **£10,539 outside London**.

London means the City of London and the 32 London boroughs, and what decides your figure is where you study, not where you live. If more than half of your course is taught in London, you use the London figure. Shorter courses are counted month by month, with a part month rounded up, so a course of six months and one week counts as seven.

### Your university accommodation deposit

A deposit paid to your university for university-arranged accommodation can come off your living costs, up to £1,529 at the time of writing, using the amount on your CAS. A deposit paid to a private hostel or student housing company does not count.

:::table
Line | Sample London course | Sample course outside London
Monthly living-cost figure | £1,529 | £1,171
Months counted for a 12-month MSc | 9 | 9
Living costs total | £13,761 | £10,539
Sample first-year tuition fee | £26,000 | £18,500
Fee deposit paid, shown on CAS | £5,000 | £5,000
Total to show | £34,761 | £24,039
:::

The tuition fees here are examples. Use the figures on your own CAS.

:::stats
£1529 | a month for London courses, at the time of writing
£1171 | a month for courses outside London
28 days | in a row the money must be held
:::

## Costs on top: visa fee and health surcharge {#costs-on-top-of-the-funds}

At the time of writing, the [Student visa fee](https://www.gov.uk/student-visa) is **£558** from outside the UK, and the [Immigration Health Surcharge](https://www.gov.uk/healthcare-immigration-application/how-much-pay) is **£776 a year** for students. The surcharge follows the length of your visa, not your course.

A course of 12 months or more usually gets up to a month of visa before it starts and four months after it ends, so a one-year master's typically means a visa of a little under 17 months. Visas over a year and up to 18 months are charged at one and a half years, which is £1,164 at the time of writing. Confirm yours with the official calculator.

## The 28-day rule and the 31-day rule {#the-28-day-and-31-day-rules}

**The 28-day rule:** the full amount must be in the account for at least 28 days in a row. In a row means every day. If an EMI or a fee payment takes the balance below target for even one day, you have to count again from the day it recovers. UKVI counts the 28 days backwards from the closing balance date on your most recent statement or letter, and your evidence must cover the whole period.

**The 31-day rule:** that most recent statement or letter must be dated no more than 31 days before you apply. The GOV.UK example: apply on 1 January, and you need to show the funds were held for at least the 28-day period ending on 1 December. Leave it longer and the evidence is too old, even if the money is still there.

:::steps
1 July: day 1 | The full amount, plus a cushion, is in the account. Move any automatic debits elsewhere. From today the balance must not fall below target.
28 July: day 28 | You have held the money for 28 days in a row. Download a statement or get a bank letter dated on or after today, covering the whole window.
28 July to 28 August: apply | Apply within 31 days of the closing balance date. If the statement closes on 28 July, 28 August is the last day. Aim for the first two weeks instead.
After you apply | Leave the money alone until you have a decision if you can. If you pay fees or a hall deposit meanwhile, keep the receipts.
:::

:::tip Make sure the statement covers the whole window
A statement that only shows the last two weeks cannot prove 28 days, even if the money has been there for months. Check that every day of your window appears.
:::

## Whose money counts

The money can be in your own name, alone or in a joint account, or in your parent's or legal guardian's name. A partner applying with you, or who already has permission, also counts. The holder must control the account and be able to withdraw the money immediately.

With a parent's account you need two extra documents: a letter from them consenting to you using the money, and proof they are your parent, usually your birth certificate showing their name. A court document naming a legal guardian also works. An affidavit alone is not proof of the relationship.

In many Indian homes the education fund is a joint effort: a grandparent's savings, an uncle's contribution, a sister's salary. That help is welcome, but it must be moved into your account or your parent's account and then sit there for the full 28 days. A sibling's account does not count, and nor does a promise of future support.

:::table
Source of money | Counts? | What you need
Your own or joint account | Yes | Statement or bank letter showing your name
Parent's or legal guardian's account | Yes | Consent letter plus birth certificate or guardianship document
Education loan in your name | Yes | Loan letter meeting the UKVI conditions
Official sponsorship, such as a government or university | Yes | Shown on your CAS, or a sponsor letter
Sibling's, relative's or friend's account | No | Move it to an eligible account, then wait 28 days
Education loan in a parent's name | No | The loan must be made to you
Overdraft or credit limit | No | Only money actually in the account counts
Shares, bonds or cryptocurrency | No | Move it to a savings account first
:::

Fixed deposits are a common question. The rules accept deposit accounts if the money can be accessed immediately, and a certificate of deposit works if the bank confirms the money was held for the 28 days and can be withdrawn at any time. If your FD has a lock-in, or the bank will not confirm access in writing, move the money to a savings account and start the clock there.

## The documents that prove it

UKVI accepts bank statements (paper or downloaded), passbooks, certificates of deposit and bank letters. There is no fixed template, but caseworker guidance says a bank record would normally:

- be printed or electronic, on official stationery, never handwritten
- show the account holder's name, and every name on a joint account
- show the account number and the date of the statement
- show the bank's details, such as contact details or a branch code
- show the balance, and ideally transactions over time

A bank letter should be on headed paper, signed by a bank official and include contact details UKVI can use to verify it. ATM mini statements are not accepted, and neither are records written or amended by hand. UKVI may check with your bank, and evidence it cannot verify can lead to refusal.

You do not convert rupees yourself. UKVI uses the spot rate on [OANDA](https://www.oanda.com) for your application date, which may differ from your bank's rate. Keep a cushion of five to ten per cent above the minimum so a weak week for the rupee does not leave you short.

### Education loan letters

The 28-day rule does not apply to a loan. Instead, the loan letter must:

- be dated no more than six months before you apply
- confirm it is a student loan from a government, a government-sponsored student loan company, or an educational loans scheme from a lender regulated for student loans
- confirm there are no conditions on release other than a successful visa application
- state the amount and confirm the loan is to you
- confirm the money will be available to you, or paid to your university, before you travel

A loan sanctioned to your father cannot count as a loan to you, and a letter saying funds will be released only after collateral is registered has a condition on it. Ask your lender for a letter written against these points. If the loan covers only part of your total, show the rest in an account that meets the 28-day rule.

### Do Indian applicants have to upload bank evidence?

Yes. At the time of writing, India is not on the GOV.UK differential evidence list of nationalities that can skip uploading financial evidence, and even those students must hold the money. Prepare the full set: statement or letter, consent letter and birth certificate if a parent holds the funds, and a loan letter if you have one.

The genuine student assessment can also look at whether your source of funds is credible and how your family came to have the money. If there is a large recent deposit, from a land sale, a matured policy or a gift, keep the paperwork and be ready to explain it.

## Mistakes that get applications refused

These slips can sink an application even when the family has the money.

- **The balance dips for a day.** Use an account with no automatic debits, and check every closing balance in the 28 days.
- **Applying before day 28.** Count from the day the money landed, not the day you asked for the transfer, and add two days of margin.
- **A statement older than 31 days.** If your appointment or application date slips, get a fresh statement.
- **Money in the wrong name.** Move a sibling's or uncle's money into your or a parent's account, then wait 28 days.
- **A parent's account with missing paperwork.** Prepare the consent letter and birth certificate alongside the statement.
- **Exactly the minimum, in rupees.** The OANDA rate on your application date decides the pound value, so hold a cushion.
- **Counting money that is not cash.** Overdrafts, shares and locked FDs do not count. Use a savings or current account.
- **A loan letter with conditions.** Pending collateral or a parent's name on the loan fails the rules. Ask for a compliant letter.
- **Deducting a deposit that does not qualify.** Only deposits paid to your university for its own housing come off.

:::warning Check the lowest balance, not the latest one
Find the single lowest closing balance in your 28-day window and convert it at the current OANDA rate. If it is below target, you are not ready to apply, however healthy today's balance looks.
:::

:::cta community

## A worked example: Ananya's numbers {#a-worked-example}

Ananya is a made-up student from Pune with an offer for a one-year MSc at a university in Leeds. Her fee is £18,500 and she has paid a £6,000 deposit, shown on her CAS. She has also paid the university £500 for a room in its own halls, also on her CAS. Her father holds the money in his savings account.

1. Leeds is outside London, so she uses £1,171 a month at the time of writing.
2. Living costs stop at nine months: 9 × £1,171 = £10,539.
3. Outstanding fees: £18,500 − £6,000 = £12,500.
4. Her hall deposit qualifies and is under the £1,529 cap: £10,539 − £500 = £10,039.
5. Total to show: £12,500 + £10,039 = **£22,539**.

Her father converts £22,539 at the OANDA rate, adds about eight per cent, and has the full rupee amount in place by 1 July. He moves his SIP and electricity bill debits to another account. On 30 July Ananya downloads a statement for 1 to 29 July, gets his signed consent letter and scans her birth certificate. She applies on 8 August, well inside 31 days.

Had she paid a private housing company instead, the £500 would not come off and her total would be £23,039, exactly the kind of gap that leaves a balance a few hundred pounds short.

> Print the statement, take a highlighter, and check the closing balance for every one of the 28 days against your target in pounds. It takes ten minutes and it is the cheapest insurance in the whole application.
> — Priya Sharma, Mentor, MSc Data Science, University of Leeds

## Before you apply: your checklist {#before-you-apply-checklist}

Tick these off the week before you submit. If any line is not true yet, fix it before you pay.

:::checklist Before you apply {#before-you-apply}
CAS checked: fee, fees already paid and any university accommodation deposit are correct
Total worked out: outstanding fees plus up to 9 months of living costs, minus any qualifying deposit
Funds in your name, a joint account with your name, or a parent's or legal guardian's account
Balance at or above target, at the OANDA rate, every day for 28 days in a row
Latest statement or bank letter dated within 31 days of your application date
Statement shows your name, account number, bank details, date and balance
Parent's signed consent letter, plus your birth certificate
Loan letter dated within six months, in your name, with no conditions other than the visa
University receipts for anything paid after the CAS was issued
Visa fee and health surcharge budgeted separately
:::

Know your number, hold it for 28 days without a single dip, apply within 31 days of the statement, and keep the money in a name that counts. Everything else is paperwork, and paperwork can be checked.
